claim: On 2024-11-20 Application and Network Load Balancers added Capacity Unit (LCU) reservation, which sets a minimum capacity for the load balancer.
q: When could you first set a minimum capacity on an Application or Network Load Balancer yourself?
values: set a minimum capacity for your load balancer
note: d116. Current truth: elb-lcu-reservation-static-minimum-capacity. The old practice (asking AWS Support to pre-warm) is stated on no saved AWS page; the 2024 What's New post is blocked by robots.txt, so no old value is recorded.

claim: On 2025-04-10 Gateway Load Balancers added LCU reservation, to set a minimum bandwidth capacity on top of the existing automatic scaling.
q: When did Gateway Load Balancers get LCU reservation?
ev: Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) now supports Load Balancer Capacity Unit (LCU) Reservation that allows you to proactively set a minimum bandwidth capacity for your load balancer, complementing its existing ability to auto-scale based on your traffic pattern.

claim: On 2023-08-10 Network Load Balancers added security groups, which you associate with the load balancer at creation.
q: Since when can a Network Load Balancer have security groups?
values: associate security groups with your Network Load Balancers
note: d117. Older exam material may assume a Network Load Balancer has no security group. Current truth: elb-nlb-sg-only-at-creation, elb-nlb-security-groups-only-at-creation, elb-nlb-no-sg-all-traffic-allowed. The 2023 What's New post is blocked by robots.txt, so no old value is quoted.

claim: On 2023-11-26 Application Load Balancers added mutual TLS authentication.
q: When did Application Load Balancers add mutual TLS authentication?

claim: On 2025-02-28 Application Load Balancer HTTP header modification was extended to all response codes; before, it was limited to response codes 2xx and 3xx.
q: Which response codes does Application Load Balancer header modification cover, and what changed in February 2025?
note: d119. Header modification itself was announced on 2024-11-21 (What's New, robots-blocked). Current truth: elb-alb-header-modification-no-code-change.

claim: On 2025-10-15 Application Load Balancers added transforms that rewrite host headers and URLs of incoming requests before routing to a target.
q: When could an Application Load Balancer first rewrite URLs and host headers?

claim: On 2025-11-21 Application Load Balancers added validation of JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for service-to-service and machine-to-machine communication.
q: When could an Application Load Balancer first validate JWT access tokens?

claim: On 2025-11-19 Network Load Balancers added weighted target groups for the default action, for blue/green and canary deployments.
q: Since when can a Network Load Balancer split traffic across weighted target groups?
values: default action with weighted target groups
note: d120. No saved page states the old value (one target group per forward action) verbatim. Current truth: elb-nlb-weighted-default-action.
ev: Weighted target groups enables key use cases like Blue-Green and Canary Deployments, Application Migration, and A/B Testing by allowing you to register multiple target groups with configurable weights ranging from 0 to 999, providing precise control over traffic distribution.

claim: On 2025-11-13 Network Load Balancers added QUIC and TCP_QUIC protocols, forwarding QUIC traffic in passthrough mode.
q: When did Network Load Balancers add QUIC support?
ev: AWS Network Load Balancer (NLB) now supports QUIC protocol in passthrough mode, enabling low-latency forwarding of QUIC traffic while preserving session stickiness through QUIC Connection ID.

claim: On 2025-02-13 Network Load Balancers gained the ability to disable (remove) an Availability Zone of an existing load balancer; before, you could add Availability Zones but not remove them.
q: Can you remove an Availability Zone from an existing Network Load Balancer, and since when?

changed.was: customers could add AZs to an existing NLB, but could not remove AZs

ev: Prior to this launch, customers could add AZs to an existing NLB, but could not remove AZs.

claim: Network Load Balancer listener rules, which route by source IP address type on a dual-stack load balancer, appear in the NLB document history on 2026-07-10 and were announced on 2026-07-22; before, serving IPv4 and IPv6 clients with their own client IPs needed two load balancers or protocol translation.
q: What did Network Load Balancer listener rules change in July 2026, and is it examinable?
values: route connections to different target groups
either run two separate load balancers

changed.was: either run two separate load balancers (one per IP version) and split clients with DNS, or send all traffic to one target group and lose the original client IP through protocol translation

note: d121. Not examinable yet: general availability announced 2026-07-22, after the 2026-07-15 cutoff (history row 2026-07-10). Current truth: elb-nlb-listener-rules-dual-stack-source-ip-type.
ev: Previously, serving both IPv4 and IPv6 clients from one NLB meant accepting a tradeoff: either run two separate load balancers (one per IP version) and split clients with DNS, or send all traffic to one target group and lose the original client IP through protocol translation.
Network Load Balancer (NLB) now supports listener rules allowing you to route connections to different target groups based on the source IP address type.

claim: On 2026-09-24 zonal shift on cross-zone Network Load Balancers was extended to target groups with connection termination for unhealthy targets, UDP target groups and Application Load Balancer targets.
q: What did the September 2026 Network Load Balancer zonal shift update add, and is it examinable?
values: Zonal shift for additional target group configurations
scope: Network Load Balancers with cross-zone load balancing enabled
note: d131. Not examinable yet (after the 2026-07-15 cutoff).
